steps.html: Gas particles are in constant random motion; collisions are elastic (no energy lost, so they never slow down and stop).
Pressure = particles colliding with the container walls.
Average kinetic energy ∝ temperature in Kelvin; individual particles can still change speed.
Particles are assumed to take up no volume and have no attractions, so gases behave best at high T and low P.
Same temperature → same average kinetic energy. KE = ½mv², so lighter = faster.
Compare molar masses from the periodic table; the smallest molar mass has the highest average velocity.
Boyle: P and V are inverse (V up → P down) at constant T, n.
Charles: V and T (K) are direct (T down → V down) at constant P, n.
Gay-Lussac: P and T (K) are direct. Avogadro: V and n are direct; more moles in a fixed container → more pressure.
1 atm = 760 mmHg = 760 torr = 101.325 kPa (exact, so they don't limit sig figs).
1 L = 1000 mL. Set it up by factor label so the old unit cancels.
Any gas equation with a temperature in it needs Kelvin.
Combined gas law: P and V units only have to match each other.
PV = nRT: P must be atm and V must be L (because R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K)).
P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. Cross out anything held constant (same T → Boyle P₁V₁ = P₂V₂; same P → Charles V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂).
Temperatures in Kelvin (°C + 273.15). P and V just need matching units.
Rearrange for the unknown, plug in everything at once, don't round early.
Asked for °C? Convert your Kelvin answer back (− 273.15). The Kelvin number is usually a trap choice.
Sanity check: smaller volume → higher pressure; hotter → bigger volume or pressure.
Lighter gases move faster, so they escape a pinhole (effuse) and spread (diffuse) faster.
Compare molar masses: the smallest one escapes in the largest amount.
At the same T and P, equal moles occupy equal volumes, whatever the gas.
Volume ∝ moles: twice the moles → twice the volume; 1 mol + 1 mol → twice the volume of 1 mol.
Equal grams are NOT equal moles (different molar masses). One molar mass of each = 1 mol each.
PV = nRT is an approximation. It works best at low pressure and high temperature.
Real gases deviate because the particles attract each other and occupy some volume.
PV = nRT, R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K).
Convert first: P → atm (÷ 760 from mmHg), V → L (÷ 1000 from mL), T → K (+ 273.15), grams → moles.
Grams of an element gas? Check if it's diatomic (H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂) before using the molar mass.
Rearrange: P = nRT/V, V = nRT/P, n = PV/RT, T = PV/nR. A T answer comes out in Kelvin.
Gas STP = 0 °C (273.15 K) and 1 atm.
At STP, 1 mol of any gas = 22.4 L; use it as a factor (22.4 L / 1 mol).

molar-density.title: Molar mass and density of a gas

steps.html: Molar mass = grams ÷ moles; get the moles from n = PV/RT (or M = mRT/PV in one step).
Density d = PM/(RT) in g/L.
Write and balance the reaction; the coefficients are the mole ratio.
Factor label: grams → moles (molar mass) → mole ratio → moles of the gas.
Then PV = nRT for V or P, or 22.4 L/mol if it's at STP.
When every substance is a gas at the same T and P, liters follow the coefficient ratio just like moles.
Given L × (coefficient wanted / coefficient given) = L wanted.
P_total = P_A + P_B + P_C + …
Every pressure must be in the same unit before you add (1 atm = 760 mmHg).
Mixture in one container: add the moles and use PV = n_total RT.
Gases mixing into a bigger volume: each one expands first (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂), then add.
X_A = mol A ÷ total mol (no unit; all the X's add to 1).
P_A = X_A × P_total.
Kinetic = energy of motion. Potential = stored, due to position or composition.
q = heat. First law: energy can't be created or destroyed; it transfers or changes form.
Heat flows hot → cold. The object gaining heat is +q; the one losing heat is −q.
Some reactions absorb energy (endothermic) and some release it (exothermic); phase changes always involve energy.
Course key: "Temperature measures heat energy" is graded true.
Specific heat c = J needed to warm 1 g by 1 °C. Higher c → smaller temperature change for the same heat.
Higher c also means it takes in more heat to warm up and gives off more heat as it cools.
Values from the problem or table: water 4.184, Al 0.897, Fe 0.449, Cu 0.385, Au 0.129, Pb ≈ 0.128 J/(g·°C).
q = m · c · ΔT, with ΔT = T_final − T_initial.
Heat absorbed: +q. Heat released (cooled): put q in as negative; ΔT is also negative, so they cancel.
Rearrange for what's missing: m = q/(cΔT), c = q/(mΔT), ΔT = q/(mc).
Mass and specific heat are never negative; a negative answer means a sign slipped.
Heat lost by the hot object = heat gained by the cold one: m·c·ΔT (metal) = m·c·ΔT (water).
Water c = 4.184 J/(g·°C); the metal's c is given.
Each ΔT is from its own start to the shared final (equilibrium) temperature. Use the sizes (positive) on both sides.
Solve the one unknown: a mass, a specific heat or a starting temperature.
Enthalpy (ΔH): heat for a specific number of moles (the reaction as written), in kJ or kJ/mol.
Heat energy (q): total heat in and out of a system, usually in J.
Exothermic: releases heat, ΔH negative, heat written as a product (right side).
Endothermic: absorbs heat, ΔH positive, heat written as a reactant (left side).
Energy written inside an equation is always added (+), never subtracted.
Thermodynamic standard state: 25 °C and 1 atm.
Gas STP: 0 °C and 1 atm. The temperatures are different.
ΔH = heat (kJ) ÷ moles of the substance with coefficient 1 in the reaction.
Heat in J? Divide by 1000 first.
Sign: released → negative, absorbed → positive.
ΔH is a conversion factor: (|ΔH| kJ / coefficient mol of that substance).
grams → moles (molar mass) → kJ, or kJ → moles → grams, by factor label.
The sign tells direction: negative = heat produced/released.
ΔH_f° = 0 only for an element in its standard state at 25 °C (O₂ g, H₂ g, N₂ g, Br₂ l, Hg l, metals s).
Compounds, lone atoms of diatomic elements and other phases are not zero.
Makes exactly 1 mole of the compound.
From its elements in their standard states (diatomic gases as X₂; no ions, no lone atoms).
Use fractions (½ O₂, 3/2 H₂) to keep the product at 1 mol.
ΔH_rxn = Σ n·ΔH_f(products) − Σ n·ΔH_f(reactants) ("products minus reactants").
Multiply each ΔH_f by its coefficient; standard-state elements are 0.
Solving for an unknown ΔH_f? Plug in ΔH_rxn and solve the same equation for it.
Reverse an equation → flip the sign of ΔH.
Multiply an equation (×2, ×½…) → multiply ΔH by the same number.
Arrange the given equations so the target's reactants are on the left and products on the right; anything on both sides cancels; add the ΔH's.

problems.q: Which statements are true about the Kinetic Molecular Theory?
problems.answer: Individual gas molecules may change speeds over time.; Pressure is a result of the collisions of gas particles hitting the sides of the container in which they are housed.; The kinetic energy of a sample of gas is proportional to the temperature in Kelvin. This means that gas molecules in a sample that is hot will move faster than gas molecules in a sample that is cooler.; Gases are assumed to not take up any space relative to size of the container.

steps.html: True: molecules can change speed (collisions trade energy), pressure comes from wall collisions, KE ∝ T in Kelvin, and particles are assumed to take no space.
False: collisions are elastic, so they never slow down and stop; gases are most ideal at high temperature, not low.

problems.q: Select the gas with the highest average velocity at 298 K.

steps.html: Molar masses: H₂ = 2.02, H₂O = 18.02, O₂ = 32.00, CO₂ = 44.01 g/mol.
Same temperature (298 K) → same average KE, so the lightest gas is fastest → hydrogen.

problems.q: On the left is a magnified view of a very small portion of liquid water in a closed container. Which magnified view would best represent what it looks like after the water evaporates?

steps.html: Evaporation is a physical change: the H₂O molecules stay intact (one O with two H).
As a gas the molecules are far apart, so there are only a few in the magnified circle.
Picture 2 shows H₂ and O₂ (water broke apart: wrong), Picture 4 is still packed like a liquid, Picture 3 is empty → Picture 5.

problems.q: What would 26.4 ºF be in ºC?
FLASHBACK: Convert 197.1 °F to Celsius. Round your answer to 1 decimal.
Convert 50.77 °C to Kelvin. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.
Convert 49.91 °C to Kelvin. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.
Which statements are true?
problems.answer: As volume increases pressure will decrease.; As you decrease the temperature of a gas, the volume will decrease.; Volume of a gas is directly proportional to temperature in Kelvin at constant pressure and number of moles.

steps.html: True: volume up → pressure down (Boyle); temperature down → volume down (Charles); V ∝ T in Kelvin.
False: V is inversely (not directly) proportional to P; more moles → more pressure, not less.

problems.q: If a gas is measured to be 980.5 torr (980.5 mmHg), what would the pressure be in atm? (Don't lose any sig figs!)

steps.html: 1 atm = 760 torr (exact).
980.5 torr × (1 atm / 760 torr) = 1.290 atm
980.5 has 4 sig figs → keep 4: 1.290 atm (the trailing 0 counts).

problems.q: If a gas is measured to be 329 kPa, what would the pressure be in atm? (Don't lose any sig figs!)

steps.html: 329 kPa × (1 atm / 101.325 kPa) = 3.25 atm

problems.q: FLASHBACK: If a gas is measured to be 302.1 mL, what would the volume be in L? (Don't lose any sig figs!)

steps.html: 302.1 mL × (1 L / 1000 mL) = 0.3021 L

problems.q: Answer yes or no for each.

steps.html: Temperature always in Kelvin → yes.
Combined gas law: P units only have to match → no; V units only have to match → no.

problems.q: A 12.4 L cylinder contains a sample of gas at 2.54 atm. What pressure would the gas be in a 10.6 L cylinder at this same temperature?

steps.html: Same temperature → Boyle: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
Check: the volume shrank, so the pressure should go up (2.97 > 2.54). ✓

problems.q: A 13.3 L cylinder contains a sample of gas at 14.5 atm. What pressure would the gas be in a 7.3 L cylinder at this same temperature? Report your answer in atmospheres to the ones position.

steps.html: Same temperature → P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.

problems.q: A gas with a pressure of 435 mmHg and a volume of 25.1 mL has a pressure change to 401.1 mmHg at constant temperature. What is the new volume of the gas?

steps.html: Constant temperature → P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. Both pressures are mmHg, so no conversion.

problems.q: A gas volume is 64.91 L at 8.747 atm. The pressure of the gas changed to 1.409 atm at the same temperature. What is the final volume of the gas? (For full credit: correct sig figs and the unit.)

steps.html: Same temperature → P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.

problems.q: A gas with a temperature of 28 ºC and a volume of 23.5 mL is contracted to 14.6 mL at constant pressure. What is the new temperature of the gas?

steps.html: Constant pressure → Charles: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂, T in Kelvin.
Back to °C: 187.1 − 273.15 = −86 °C (187 is the Kelvin trap).

problems.q: A sample of gas initially at 160.0 mmHg and occupying 25.0 mL at 307.15 K is cooled to 299.15 K and expanded to 160.0 mL. What is the final pressure of the sample of gas?

steps.html: All three change → P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ → P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁). Temperatures are already Kelvin.

problems.q: A sample of gas initially at 160.0 mmHg and occupying 25.0 mL at 34 °C is cooled to 26.0 °C and expanded to 160.0 mL. What is the final pressure of the sample of gas?

steps.html: Same numbers as the previous problem: P₂ = 160.0 × (25.0/160.0) × (299.15/307.15) = 24.3 mmHg

problems.q: A 43.17 mL container holds gas initially at 11.65 °C and 253.7 torr. If the volume changes to 57.07 mL and the temperature changes to 26.3 °C, what is the final pressure of this gas in torr? Don't round early! Report your answer to four significant figures.

steps.html: P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁); mL and torr can stay.

problems.q: A sample of gas initially occupies 238 mL at 126 °C and 946 mmHg. What is the volume if the gas is cooled to 94 °C and the pressure is decreased to 547 mmHg?

steps.html: V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁).

problems.q: A sample of gas in a 28.5 L container is initially at 15 °C and 701 mmHg. If the pressure is reduced to 479 mmHg and the temperature is increased to 75 °C, what is the final volume? Add 273 to convert to Kelvin. Report your answer in liters to three significant figures.

steps.html: V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁). The problem says add 273.

problems.q: A sample of gas occupies 459 mL at 44.5 °C and 658 torr. What is the temperature if the gas is compressed to 250 mL and the pressure is changed to 759 torr?

steps.html: T₂ = T₁ × (P₂V₂)/(P₁V₁), with T₁ in Kelvin. The answer choices were built with 273.
Back to °C: 199.5 − 273 = −73.5 °C (199.5 is the Kelvin trap; 273.15 gives −73.6, closest choice is still −73.5).

problems.q: If a mixture with equal moles of helium gas and neon gas is allowed to escape through a pinhole in a container, the escaping gas would contain more neon than helium.

steps.html: He = 4.00 g/mol, Ne = 20.18 g/mol.
Lighter escapes faster, so the escaping gas has more helium → statement is False.

problems.q: Which of the following is NOT true about helium gas and argon gas samples at the same temperature and pressure?
choices: 4.00 grams of helium will occupy the same volume as 39.95 grams of argon.
The same number of moles of each will occupy the same volume.
If you have twice as many moles of argon as helium, the volume of argon will be twice as large.
The same number of grams of each will occupy the same volume.
One mole each of helium and argon in a container will take up twice the volume of 1 mole of helium by itself.
problems.answer: The same number of grams of each will occupy the same volume.

steps.html: 4.00 g He = 1 mol and 39.95 g Ar = 1 mol, so those occupy the same volume (true).
Equal moles → equal volume; twice the moles → twice the volume; 1 + 1 mol → twice 1 mol (all true).
Equal grams are different numbers of moles → "The same number of grams of each will occupy the same volume" is NOT true.

problems.q: The ideal gas law equation is an approximation of a more complicated equation. It has the best results for molecules that are at low pressure and high temperature.

steps.html: Low pressure (particles far apart) and high temperature (fast, attractions matter less) → True.

problems.q: Gases do not obey the ideal gas law perfectly because the gas particles do interact and they also do occupy a small portion of the volume of the container.

steps.html: Real particles do attract and do take up space, the two things the ideal model ignores → True.

problems.q: What pressure is exerted by 3.25 grams of nitrogen gas in a 1.50 L container at 52.0 °C? (Hint: Will you use N or N₂?)

steps.html: Nitrogen gas is diatomic: N₂ = 2 × 14.01 = 28.02 g/mol.
3.25 g N₂ × (1 mol N₂ / 28.02 g N₂) = 0.1160 mol N₂

problems.q: What is the correct value of R as well as temperature for GASES?
choices: R = 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) and T should be in Kelvin ALWAYS.
R = 0.821 L*atm/(mol*K) and T should be in Kelvin ALWAYS.
R = 8.314 L*atm/(mol*K) and T should be in Kelvin ALWAYS.
R = 8.314 L*atm/(mol*K) and T should be in Celsius ALWAYS.
R = 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) and T should be in Celsius ALWAYS.
problems.answer: R = 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) and T should be in Kelvin ALWAYS.

steps.html: R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) and T in Kelvin always. (8.314 is R in J/(mol·K).)

problems.q: Fill in each blank.

steps.html: Gas STP: 0.00 °C = 273.15 K and 1.0 atm.
Temperature in Kelvin for every gas calculation → yes.
Combined gas law: P and V units just match → no, no.
PV = nRT needs atm and L (because of R) → yes.

problems.q: What pressure in atm will 0.125 moles of a gas occupy at 231 mL and 195 °C? (R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) · correct sig figs and units.)
What volume will 0.700 moles of helium gas occupy at 0.944 atm and 15.0 °C?
What size container (in L) will a gas occupy if 0.55 moles are added so that the gas is at STP? (Use the correct number of sig figs and the correct unit.)

steps.html: At STP, 1 mol = 22.4 L.
0.55 mol × (22.4 L / 1 mol) = 12.3 L
0.55 has 2 sig figs → 12 L.

problems.q: A sample of nitrogen gas is confined to a 14.0 L container at 0.493 atm and 37 °C. How many moles of nitrogen are in the container?
A gas fills a 22.4 L container and it is sealed when the gas measures being at STP. How many moles are in the container? The answer should have 1 decimal place.

steps.html: At STP, 22.4 L is exactly 1 mol → 1.0 mol.

problems.q: 1.95 moles of a gas will occupy 41.2 L. The pressure is measured to be 2.45 atm. What is the temperature in °C? Round to the ones position. (R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K))

steps.html: PV = nRT gives Kelvin. °C = 630.5 − 273.15 = 357 °C

problems.q: What is the molar mass of a gas if a flask with a volume of 3.16 L contains 9.33 grams of the gas at 32.0 °C and 1.00 atm?

steps.html: M = grams ÷ moles = 9.33 ÷ 0.1261 = 74.0 g/mol

problems.q: What is the molar mass of a gas if 1.89 grams of the gas in a 0.539 L flask at 299 K has a pressure of 1.151 atm? Report to three significant figures. (Use R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K).)
Determine the density in g/L of a gas with a molar mass of 65.17 g/mol at 319 K and 15.5 atm. (R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K))

steps.html: d = PM/(RT).

problems.q: Potassium chlorate decomposes to produce potassium chloride and oxygen. What volume of oxygen would be collected at 22.0 °C and 728 mmHg by the decomposition of 8.15 g of potassium chlorate? (Write and balance the reaction first.)

steps.html: Balanced: 2 KClO₃ → 2 KCl + 3 O₂.
8.15 g KClO₃ × (1 mol KClO₃ / 122.55 g KClO₃) × (3 mol O₂ / 2 mol KClO₃) = 0.09976 mol O₂

problems.q: Nitrogen reacts with oxygen to form dinitrogen trioxide: 2 N₂ + 3 O₂ → 2 N₂O₃. What pressure of oxygen is required to produce 1.648 grams of dinitrogen trioxide in a 2.64 L container at 274 K?

steps.html: 1.648 g N₂O₃ × (1 mol N₂O₃ / 76.02 g N₂O₃) × (3 mol O₂ / 2 mol N₂O₃) = 0.03252 mol O₂

problems.q: 2 N₂ + 3 O₂ → 2 N₂O₃. What pressure of oxygen is required to produce 3.3 grams of dinitrogen trioxide in a 7.7 L container at 321.00 K? (R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) · molar mass of N₂O₃ = 76.01 g/mol)

steps.html: 3.3 g N₂O₃ × (1 mol N₂O₃ / 76.01 g N₂O₃) × (3 mol O₂ / 2 mol N₂O₃) = 0.06512 mol O₂
3.3 and 7.7 have 2 sig figs → 0.22 atm

problems.q: At STP, this reaction occurred: XY (g) + 3 AB (aq) → A₃Y (g) + B₃X (s). How many liters of gas are produced from 2.6 grams of AB? (You may or may not need all of this: molar mass AB = 58.21 g/mol · correct sig figs and unit.)

steps.html: At STP, 1 mol gas = 22.4 L. The only gas produced is A₃Y (1 per 3 AB).
2.6 g AB × (1 mol AB / 58.21 g AB) × (1 mol A₃Y / 3 mol AB) × (22.4 L / 1 mol A₃Y) = 0.33 L

problems.q: A gas phase reaction at constant temperature and pressure in a flexible container: A₂Z (g) + 2 X (g) → 2 AX (g) + Z (g). If 2.29 L of A₂Z react with excess X, how many liters of AX will form?

steps.html: All gases at constant T and P → liters follow the coefficients.
2.29 L A₂Z × (2 L AX / 1 L A₂Z) = 4.58 L AX

problems.q: Five gases are mixed into one container. The partial pressures are A = 0.78 atm, B = 1.20 atm, C = 2.43 atm, D = 0.46 atm, E = 1.57 atm. What is the total pressure in atm? Round to the hundredths place.
Three gases are mixed into one container. Partial pressures: A = 880.1 mmHg, B = 0.59 atm, C = 3.66 atm. What is the total pressure in atm? Round to the hundredths place.

steps.html: Units first: 880.1 mmHg ÷ 760 = 1.158 atm.

problems.q: Three gases, A, B and C, are in one container with a total pressure of 739.1 mmHg. A = 135.1 mmHg and B = 385.3 mmHg. What is the partial pressure of gas C in mmHg? Round to the tenths place.

steps.html: P_C = P_total − P_A − P_B

problems.q: If 0.56 moles of radon and 0.73 moles of hydrogen are placed in a 3.7 L container at 235 °C, what pressure does the mixture exert?

steps.html: Mixture: add the moles, then PV = nRT.

problems.q: If 1.79 moles of argon and 1.15 moles of oxygen are placed in a 4.31 L container at 39.3 °C, what is the total pressure of the mixture? (R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) · correct sig figs and units.)

What is the total pressure of this mixture? Helium at 145 mmHg is in a 3.00 L container at 28 ºC, and argon at 355 mmHg is in a 2.00 L container at 28 ºC. The two containers are connected and opened to each other at constant temperature, so the total volume is now 5.00 L.

steps.html: Each gas expands into the full 5.00 L (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂), then add.
Total = 87 + 142 = 229 mmHg

problems.q: A mixture of gas contains 3.00 g of element A and 3.00 g of element B. A has a molar mass of 39.1 g/mol and B has a molar mass of 45.1 g/mol. What is the mole fraction of element A?

Four gases, A, B, C and D, are mixed into a sealed container with a total pressure of 3.06 atm. The mole fractions are A = 0.10, B = 0.20, C = 0.30, D = 0.40. What is the partial pressure of gas A? Report the correct number of sig figs.

steps.html: P_A = X_A × P_total

problems.q: BONUS: Hydrochloric acid is prepared by bubbling hydrogen chloride gas through water. What is the concentration of a solution prepared by dissolving 225 L of HCl(g) at 37 °C and 0.884 atm in enough water to make a 5.25 L solution?

steps.html: Molarity = mol ÷ L of solution.
M = 7.81 ÷ 5.25 = 1.49 M (7.82 is the moles, a trap)

problems.q: Mark the true statements below.
problems.answer: The symbol 'q' represents heat energy.; Energy cannot be created or destroyed.; Some chemical reactions will absorb energy while others release energy.; Temperature measures heat energy.; Energy can change forms such as when it changes from heat energy to chemical energy.

steps.html: True: q is heat; energy can't be created or destroyed; some reactions absorb and some release energy; energy changes forms; and (course key) temperature measures heat energy.
False: kinetic energy is energy of motion; thermodynamics isn't about "changing volume"; phase changes do transfer energy.

problems.q: The first law of thermodynamics tells us that the amount of energy in the universe is constant and can neither be destroyed nor created. It can be transferred or change form.

steps.html: That's the first law of thermodynamics (conservation of energy) → True.

problems.q: A cold piece of metal is placed in boiling water. Which statement is true?
choices: The metal has a relative +q value and the water has a −q value. Heat will flow from the hot water to the cold metal.
The metal has a relative −q value and the water has a +q value. Heat will flow from the hot water to the cold metal.
The metal has a relative +q value and the water has a −q value. Heat will flow from the cold metal to hot water.
The metal has a relative −q value and the water has a +q value. Heat will flow from the cold metal to hot water.
problems.answer: The metal has a relative +q value and the water has a −q value. Heat will flow from the hot water to the cold metal.

steps.html: Heat flows hot → cold: from the boiling water into the cold metal.
The metal gains heat (+q), the water loses heat (−q) → first choice.

problems.q: Kinetic energy is energy due to composition or position.

steps.html: Composition or position is potential energy; kinetic is motion → False.

problems.q: Select the true statement(s):
problems.answer: Water has a higher specific heat capacity than lead and both start at the same temperature. That means the water will need to absorb more heat energy than the lead to increase by the same temperature.

steps.html: Statement 1: higher c needs more heat for the same ΔT → true.
Statement 2: higher c releases more heat cooling the same amount → false.
Statement 3: Al c = 0.897, Fe c = 0.449. Same 100 J → iron (lower c) warms more, so iron is hotter → false.

problems.q: You have a 17.0 gram sample of gold at 20.0 °C. How much heat does it take to raise the temperature to 101.0 °C? (Specific heat of gold = 0.129 J/(g·°C) · 3 sig figs, unit abbreviation.)

An unknown mass of gold at 12.0 °C absorbs 7.83 J of energy. The final temperature is 25.0 °C. What mass of gold, in grams, is required to do this? (Specific heat of gold = 0.129 J/(g·°C). ΔT = 13.0 (3 sig figs).)

Two specific heat values: 0.689 J/g·°C and 0.341 J/g·°C. Type the specific heat value that will let the substance undergo a SMALL change in temperature when absorbing the same amount of heat as the other.

steps.html: ΔT = q ÷ (mc): the larger c gives the smaller ΔT → 0.689 J/(g*C)

problems.q: 18.0 grams of a metal at 29.5 °C was heated to 116.9 °C. Determine the amount of heat (in J) absorbed or released if the specific heat capacity of the metal is 0.185 J/(g·°C).
11.0 grams of a metal at 25.9 °C was heated to 110.9 °C. Determine the amount of heat (in J) absorbed or released if the specific heat capacity of the metal is 0.167 J/(g·°C).
A metal with a specific heat of 0.157 J/(g·°C) was heated from 39.7 °C to 109.3 °C. If 395 J were absorbed, what was the mass of the metal?
A metal with a specific heat of 0.165 J/(g·°C) was COOLED from 117.7 °C to 34.5 °C. If 349 J were released, what was the mass of the metal?

steps.html: ΔT = 34.5 − 117.7 = −83.2 °C; heat released → q = −349 J

problems.q: 202.7 J of heat were released when 13.5 grams of the substance at 114.3 °C was cooled to 20.1 °C. Determine the specific heat capacity of the metal in J/(g·°C).
A 20.0 g sample of aluminum absorbs 150 J of energy. If the initial temperature of the Al is 75.0 °C, what is the final temperature?

steps.html: Aluminum c = 0.897 J/(g·°C).
Absorbed → warmer: 75.0 + 8.36 = 83.4 °C (8.36 alone is the ΔT trap)

problems.q: A 13.0 gram sample of iron is initially at 414.0 °C. It loses 169.0 J of heat to its surroundings. What is its final temperature? Enter your answer in °C with one decimal place. (Specific heat of iron = 0.449 J/(g·°C))

A piece of copper at 98.3 °C is placed in a calorimeter containing 32.3 grams of water at 23.1 °C. If the temperature at equilibrium is 28.1 °C, what is the mass of the copper? Report two sig figs. (Specific heat of copper = 0.385 J/(g·°C) · water = 4.184 J/(g·°C))

A 34.7 gram piece of lead at 97.7 °C is placed in a calorimeter containing water at 21.9 °C. If the temperature at equilibrium is 27.6 °C, what is the mass of the water? Report two sig figs. (Specific heat of lead = 0.130 J/(g·°C))

A 34.6 gram piece of lead at 104.6 °C is placed in a calorimeter containing 30.4 grams of an unknown liquid at 22.4 °C. If the temperature at equilibrium is 29.7 °C, what is the specific heat capacity of the liquid? (Specific heat of lead = 0.129 J/(g·°C))

A 70.7 g piece of metal at 164.3 °C is placed in a calorimeter containing 171 grams of water at 26.2 °C. If the temperature at equilibrium is 31.5 °C, what was the specific heat of the metal in J/(g·°C)? Round to three decimal places.

A 66.1 g piece of metal at 164.7 °C is placed in a calorimeter containing 171 grams of water. If the temperature at equilibrium is 30.7 °C, what was the initial temperature of the water? Round to the tenths position. (Specific heat of the metal = 0.677 J/(g·°C))

steps.html: The water warmed up to 30.7, so it started at 30.7 − 8.38 = 22.3 °C

problems.q: Match the terms.
problems.answer: describes heat energy transfer for a specific number of moles in a system → enthalpy; symbol is ΔH → enthalpy; typically has a unit of joules → heat energy; describes the sum of all heat transferred into and out of a system → heat energy; symbol is q → heat energy; typically has a unit of kJ or kJ/mol → enthalpy

steps.html: Enthalpy: heat for a specific number of moles, symbol ΔH, unit kJ or kJ/mol.
Heat energy: sum of all heat in and out, symbol q, unit joules.

problems.q: Which of the following is a correct statement for a chemical reaction that absorbs heat?
choices: The reaction is exothermic with a positive ΔH.
The reaction is endothermic with a negative ΔH.
The reaction is endothermic with ΔH = 0.
The reaction is endothermic with a positive ΔH.
The reaction is exothermic with a negative ΔH.
problems.answer: The reaction is endothermic with a positive ΔH.

steps.html: Absorbs heat = endothermic = positive ΔH.

problems.q: Where would you write the word 'heat' in these equations?
problems.answer: H₂ (g) + Cl₂ (g) → 2 HCl (g)   ΔH = −184.6 kJ → to the RIGHT of the arrow; C₃H₈ (g) + 5 O₂ (g) → 3 CO₂ (g) + 4 H₂O (l)   ΔH = 2219.2 kJ → to the LEFT of the arrow; 2 CO₂ (g) → 2 CO (g) + O₂ (g)   ΔH = 566.0 kJ → to the LEFT of the arrow; 4 HCl (g) + O₂ (g) → 2 H₂O + 2 Cl₂ (g)   ΔH = −202.5 kJ → to the RIGHT of the arrow

steps.html: Negative ΔH → heat is a product (right); positive ΔH → heat is a reactant (left).
H₂ + Cl₂ (−184.6): right. C₃H₈ (+2219.2 as written): left. 2 CO₂ (+566.0): left. 4 HCl (−202.5): right.

problems.q: Label each reaction exothermic or endothermic.
problems.answer: H₂ (g) + Cl₂ (g) → 2 HCl (g)   ΔH = −184.6 kJ → exothermic; 2 CO₂ (g) → 2 CO (g) + O₂ (g)   ΔH = 566.0 kJ → endothermic; C₃H₈ (g) + 5 O₂ (g) → 3 CO₂ (g) + 4 H₂O (l)   ΔH = 2219.2 kJ → endothermic; 4 HCl (g) + O₂ (g) → 2 H₂O + 2 Cl₂ (g)   ΔH = −202.5 kJ → exothermic

steps.html: Negative ΔH = exothermic; positive ΔH = endothermic.
H₂ + Cl₂: exo. 2 CO₂: endo. C₃H₈ (+2219.2 as written): endo. 4 HCl: exo.

problems.q: The energy has been written into each equation. Which are correctly written?
problems.answer: 2 CO₂ (g) − 566.0 kJ → 2 CO (g) + O₂ (g)   ΔH = 566.0 kJ → incorrectly written; 4 HCl (g) + O₂ (g) → 2 H₂O + 2 Cl₂ (g) − 202.5 kJ   ΔH = −202.5 kJ → incorrectly written; H₂ (g) + Cl₂ (g) → 2 HCl (g) + 184.6 kJ   ΔH = −184.6 kJ → correctly written; C₃H₈ (g) + 5 O₂ (g) + 2219.2 kJ → 3 CO₂ (g) + 4 H₂O (l)   ΔH = 2219.2 kJ → correctly written

steps.html: Energy inside an equation is always +, on the left for endothermic and on the right for exothermic.
"2 CO₂ − 566.0 kJ" and "… − 202.5 kJ" use minus signs → incorrect.
"… → 2 HCl + 184.6 kJ" (exo, right) and "C₃H₈ + … + 2219.2 kJ →" (endo, left) → correct.

problems.q: Flashback: standard conditions for thermodynamics.

steps.html: Thermodynamic standard: 25 °C and 1 atm.
Gas STP is 0 °C, so the temperatures are not the same → no.

problems.q: If 163.2 g of a new chemical 'ACO₂' is produced by AC + O₂ → ACO₂ and that reaction releases 517.2 kJ of energy, what is the enthalpy change (kJ)? (ACO₂ molar mass = 184.2 g/mol)

steps.html: 163.2 g ACO₂ × (1 mol ACO₂ / 184.2 g ACO₂) = 0.8860 mol ACO₂
ΔH = −517.2 kJ ÷ 0.8860 mol = −583.8 kJ (negative: released)

problems.q: If 0.9781 g of 'XY₂' is produced by X + 2Y → XY₂ and that reaction absorbs 736.2 J of energy, what is the enthalpy change in kJ (correct sig figs)? (XY₂ molar mass = 308.21 g/mol · watch the J → kJ unit!)

steps.html: 0.9781 g XY₂ × (1 mol XY₂ / 308.21 g XY₂) = 0.003173 mol XY₂
ΔH = +0.7362 kJ ÷ 0.003173 mol = 232.0 kJ (positive: absorbed)

problems.q: 2 SO₃ (g) → 2 SO₂ (g) + O₂ (g) has an enthalpy change of 198 kJ. How many grams of sulfur dioxide are produced when 564 kJ is absorbed?

steps.html: SO₂ = 32.06 + 2(16.00) = 64.06 g/mol; 198 kJ goes with 2 mol SO₂.
564 kJ × (2 mol SO₂ / 198 kJ) × (64.06 g SO₂ / 1 mol SO₂) = 365 g SO₂

problems.q: 4 NO + 6 H₂O → 4 NH₃ + 5 O₂ has an enthalpy change of 46.72 kJ. How many grams of ammonia can be produced if 32.5 kJ of heat energy are provided? Three sig figs. (NH₃ molar mass = 17.04 g/mol)

steps.html: 32.5 kJ × (4 mol NH₃ / 46.72 kJ) × (17.04 g NH₃ / 1 mol NH₃) = 47.4 g NH₃

problems.q: 2 H₂ (g) + O₂ (g) → 2 H₂O (l) has ΔH_rxn = −571 kJ. What is the enthalpy change if 1.00 gram of hydrogen reacts in this manner?

steps.html: 1.00 g H₂ × (1 mol H₂ / 2.02 g H₂) × (−571 kJ / 2 mol H₂) = −141 kJ

problems.q: 2 AB + 5/2 O₂ → 2 AO₂ + B₂O has ΔH = −465.8 kJ. How many kJ of heat are produced when 6.27 grams of AB combust? Three sig figs. (AB molar mass = 65.0 g/mol)

steps.html: 6.27 g AB × (1 mol AB / 65.0 g AB) × (465.8 kJ / 2 mol AB) = 22.5 kJ
ΔH is negative, so 22.5 kJ is produced.

problems.q: Select the ΔH_f values that would be zero.

steps.html: Standard states at 25 °C: oxygen gas, hydrogen gas, zinc solid, bromine liquid, neon gas, nitrogen gas, calcium solid.
Zero: O₂ (g), H₂ (g), Zn (s). N₂ (l), Br₂ (s), Ca (l), Ne (s) are the wrong phase.

problems.q: Which two answers show correct set-ups for C₂H₄ (g) + 3 O₂ (g) → 2 H₂O (l) + 2 CO₂ (g)?
problems.answer: Hrxn = 2·Hf H₂O + 2·Hf CO₂ − (Hf C₂H₄ + 3·Hf O₂); Hrxn = 2·Hf H₂O + 2·Hf CO₂ − (Hf C₂H₄ + 0)

steps.html: Products minus reactants, each × coefficient: 2·H₂O + 2·CO₂ − (C₂H₄ + 3·O₂).
O₂ is a standard-state element (ΔH_f = 0), so writing 0 for it is the same set-up → the first two.

problems.q: Given A → B (ΔH = 70 kJ) and B → C (ΔH = −110 kJ), find each. Enter like "35 kJ".

steps.html: 10 B → 10 A: reverse (−70) and × 10 = −700 kJ

problems.q: Given A → B (ΔH = −50 kJ) and B → C (ΔH = 20 kJ), combine them. Enter like "35 kJ".
What is the enthalpy change for 2 Cr (s) + 3 O₂ (g) → 2 CrO₃ (s)? (4 Cr (s) + 3 O₂ (g) → 2 Cr₂O₃ (s), ΔH = −2256.8 kJ · 2 Cr₂O₃ (s) + 3 O₂ (g) → 4 CrO₃ (s), ΔH = −108.2 kJ)

steps.html: Add the two: 4 Cr + 6 O₂ → 4 CrO₃ (the 2 Cr₂O₃ cancels), ΔH = −2256.8 + (−108.2) = −2365.0 kJ
Target is half of that: −2365.0 ÷ 2 = −1182.5 kJ

problems.q: Determine the enthalpy change for 2 E + X₂ → 2 EX. Round to the ones position and include the unit. (E + X₂ → EX₂, ΔH = −544 kJ · 2 EX₂ → 2 EX + X₂, ΔH = 521 kJ)

steps.html: ×2 eq. 1: 2 E + 2 X₂ → 2 EX₂, ΔH = −1088 kJ
Keep eq. 2: 2 EX₂ → 2 EX + X₂, ΔH = 521 kJ
Add (2 EX₂ and one X₂ cancel): 2 E + X₂ → 2 EX, ΔH = −1088 + 521 = −567 kJ

problems.q: What is the enthalpy change for 4 NH₃ (g) + 5 O₂ (g) → 4 NO (g) + 6 H₂O (l)? (N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, ΔH = −922.22 kJ · N₂ + O₂ → 2 NO, ΔH = 180.5 kJ · 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (l), ΔH = −571.6 kJ)

steps.html: Reverse eq. 1, × 2: 4 NH₃ → 2 N₂ + 6 H₂, ΔH = +1844.44 kJ
Eq. 2 × 2: 2 N₂ + 2 O₂ → 4 NO, ΔH = +361.0 kJ
Eq. 3 × 3: 6 H₂ + 3 O₂ → 6 H₂O, ΔH = −1714.8 kJ

problems.q: Determine the enthalpy change for X + Y + 3/2 Z₂ → XYZ₃. Round to the ones position and include the unit. (XZ → X + ½ Z₂, ΔH = 549 kJ · Y + Z₂ → YZ₂, ΔH = −649 kJ · 2 XYZ₃ → 2 XZ + 2 YZ₂, ΔH = 639 kJ)

steps.html: Reverse eq. 1: X + ½ Z₂ → XZ, ΔH = −549 kJ
Keep eq. 2: Y + Z₂ → YZ₂, ΔH = −649 kJ
Reverse eq. 3 and × ½: XZ + YZ₂ → XYZ₃, ΔH = −319.5 kJ
